title: Why we love puzzles: the pleasure of the almost-known
description: A puzzle is a gap between what you know and what you nearly know — and the brain treats closing that gap as a small celebration. Here is why unfinished things nag us so sweetly.

body.heading: The itch of the information gap
paragraphs: Psychologist George Loewenstein described curiosity as an information gap: the itch you feel when you know some of a story but not the ending. A crossword clue you almost know, a detective novel at chapter twenty — the gap is uncomfortable and delightful at once, and closing it feels like scratching the itch.

Puzzles are information gaps with a guarantee: the answer exists, it fits perfectly, and you are allowed to find it. Real life rarely signs such a contract, which may be why a finished jigsaw feels so calming in an unfinished world.

body.heading: Small wins, honestly earned
paragraphs: Puzzles also pay out in instalments. Every placed piece, every crossed-off candidate, every “oh, THAT's how it works” is a small, honest success — earned by your own reasoning, not given by luck or flattery. The final piece is almost a formality; the pleasure was in the hundred small certainties along the way.

And puzzles respect your pace. Unlike a race, a puzzle waits. It does not mind being left at midnight and finished at breakfast, which makes it one of the few challenges in life that is entirely on your terms.

body.heading: Try it: notice your gap
paragraphs: Next time a puzzle hooks you, pause and name the gap precisely: “I know the edges are done; I don't know where the sky pieces belong.” Naming what is missing often shows you the next move — a trick that works on homework, arguments and stuck projects too.

Then set a puzzle for someone else and watch them feel the itch. Choosing what to reveal and what to hide is the setter's art: too much gap is frustration, too little is boredom, and the perfect gap is a gift.

takeaway: Puzzles turn curiosity into a game with a guaranteed ending: an itch you are allowed to scratch, at exactly your own speed.
